claim: Male mice exposed to fresh female urine robustly sniffed and vocalized for the first 5–10 min of the recording at a peak rate of about 4 events per second.
source: Male mice in the chamber were exposed to fresh female urine and robustly sniffed and vocalized for the first 5–10 min of the recording at a peak rate of about 4 events per second (n=6) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Directly stated experimental observation with sample size and figure reference

claim: A vocalization was classified as a narrow-band sound in the 40–120 kHz ultrasonic frequency range during a single breath.
source: A vocalization was classified as a narrow-band sound in the 40–120 kHz ultrasonic frequency range during a single breath (Figure 1A).
evidence: Definition provided for classification of vocalizations in the study

claim: The instantaneous frequency of vocalization breaths was typically between 5 and 10 Hz (mean: 7.5 Hz).
source: The instantaneous frequency of vocalization breaths was typically between 5 and 10 Hz (mean: 7.5 Hz) (Figure 1C)
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data with figure reference

claim: Vocalization breaths mostly occurred during episodes of rapid sniffs (8.5–10 Hz).
source: The instantaneous frequency of vocalization breaths was typically between 5 and 10 Hz (mean: 7.5 Hz) (Figure 1C) and mostly occurred during episodes of rapid sniffs (8.5–10 Hz) (Figure 1A and B), as previously reported (Sirotin et al., 2014; Castellucci et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by citations to prior work

claim: Vocalization breaths were slightly slower overall when compared to neighboring breaths.
source: When compared to neighboring breaths, vocalization breaths were slightly slower overall (Figure 1C)
evidence: Comparative measurement from experimental data

claim: Vocalization breaths had subtly larger inspiratory and perhaps expiratory airflow despite similar durations of each phase compared to neighboring breaths.
source: When compared to neighboring breaths, vocalization breaths were slightly slower overall (Figure 1C) with subtly larger inspiratory and perhaps expiratory airflow despite similar durations of each phase (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Comparative measurements from experimental data with figure references

claim: A vocalization breath appears mostly like a normal breath but with the addition of a nested sound pattern.
source: These data reveal that a vocalization breath appears mostly like a normal breath but with the addition of a nested sound pattern.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data comparing vocalization and non-vocalization breaths

claim: A distinct sub-program is activated within a breath to generate a vocalization.
source: This led us to hypothesize that a distinct sub-program is activated within a breath to generate a vocalization.
evidence: Hypothesis stated based on experimental observations

claim: The adult murine lexicon is composed of at least 10 USV syllable types that are defined by different, but stereotyped, patterns of pitch.
source: The adult murine lexicon is composed of at least 10 USV syllable types that are defined by different, but stereotyped, patterns of pitch.
evidence: Statement about the murine vocalization repertoire, consistent with cited literature (Grimsley et al., 2011)

claim: Most breaths contain a single syllable (88%).
source: Most breaths contain a single syllable (88%), which we define as a continuous USV event (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3)
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data

claim: Some breaths contain two (8%) or three (4%) syllables separated by >20 ms within a single breath.
source: however, on some occasions, we observed two (8%) or three (4%) syllables separated by >20 ms within a single breath (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data

claim: The structure of adult vocalizations mirrors that described in neonatal cries.
source: This structure mirrors that described in neonatal cries (Wei et al., 2022).
evidence: Comparison to previously published work

claim: Vocalizations began and ended throughout expiration.
source: Vocalizations began and ended throughout expiration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: The most common vocalizations tended to start near the onset of exhalation and ended shortly thereafter (like the up frequency modulated [fm], step down, flat, and short types).
source: the most common tended to start near the onset of exhalation and ended shortly thereafter (like the up frequency modulated [fm], step down, flat, and short types) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: Vocalizations with more intricate changes in pitch had more variable times of on- and offset (like complex, chevron, two step, multi, step up, down fm).
source: Vocalizations with more intricate changes in pitch had more variable times of on- and offset (like complex, chevron, two step, multi, step up, down fm) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: When the vocalizations occurred late in expiration, the duration of this breath phase was prolonged.
source: And lastly, when the vocalizations occurred late in expiration, the duration of this breath phase was prolonged (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: The bias of USV timing by the breath combined with the USV modulation of breath length demonstrate these programs are independent but reciprocally coupled.
source: The bias of USV timing by the breath combined with the USV modulation of breath length demonstrate these programs are independent but reciprocally coupled.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental observations about timing relationships

claim: Fluctuations in airflow speed through the larynx produce changes in the sound's pitch.
source: Fluctuations in airflow speed through the larynx produce changes in the sound's pitch.
evidence: Statement of established biophysical principle

claim: Augmenting airflow through the explanted rodent larynx increases pitch.
source: For example, augmenting airflow through the explanted rodent larynx increases pitch (Mahrt et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited experimental finding from prior work

claim: Down or up fm USVs were positively or negatively correlated with expiratory airflow, respectively (median r=0.62 and –0.46).
source: Down or up fm USVs served as simple USV examples and we found that these were positively or negatively correlated, respectively (median r=0.62 and –0.46, Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Quantitative correlation analysis from experimental data

claim: Down fm and up fm USVs were distinguished by the sound onset and offset, whereby down fm started and ended later during the expiration.
source: These two were also distinguished by the sound onset and offset, whereby down fm started and ended later during the expiration (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: The distinguishing features of down fm and up fm USVs are consistent with the sounds being produced by separate mechanisms to alter pitch, positive and negative intonation.
source: These distinguishing features are consistent with the sounds being produced by separate mechanisms to alter pitch, positive and negative intonation.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental observations

claim: Five of the eight other USV syllable types had positively shifted intonation: complex, step down, chevron, two step, and multi (median r=0.31, 0.28, 0.32, 0.19, and 0.24, respectively).
source: Five of the other eight USV syllable types had positively shifted intonation, the complex, step down, chevron, two step, and multi (median r=0.31, 0.28, 0.32, 0.19, and 0.24, respectively) (Figure 2B and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative correlation analysis from experimental data

claim: The mirrored oscillations in the breath expiratory airflow and pitch during a complex vocalization best illustrated the positively coupled relationship.
source: In particular, the mirrored oscillations in the breath expiratory airflow and pitch during a complex vocalization best illustrated the positively coupled relationship (model 1, Figure 2C).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with figure reference

claim: The up fm was the only USV with negative intonation.
source: In contrast, the up fm was the only USV with negative intonation.
evidence: Summary of correlation analysis results

claim: The r values for positively and negatively correlated USVs were not random, as they fell outside r values computed in simulated datasets composed of USVs with shuffled expiration airflow or expirations with shuffled pitch frequencies.
source: The r values for positively and negatively correlated USVs were not random, as they fell outside r values computed in simulated datasets composed of USVs with shuffled expiration airflow or expirations with shuffled pitch frequencies (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical comparison to null distributions from shuffled data

claim: The two step and step up USVs appeared to have a portion of the pitch pattern correlated with the expiratory airflow, while the other part(s) were un- or anti-correlated.
source: The two step and step up USVs (median r=0.19 and –0.03) appeared to have a portion of the pitch pattern correlated with the expiratory airflow, while the other part(s) were un- or anti-correlated (e.g. the two step, Figure 2E).
evidence: Observation from correlation analysis with figure reference

claim: The pitch of two step and step up USVs is produced by switching between positive and negative intonation mechanisms within the breath.
source: This suggests that the pitch is produced by switching between positive and negative intonation mechanisms within the breath.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation patterns observed in data

claim: Flat and short USV types occurred with various breath shapes which resulted in a wide range of r values.
source: The remaining two USV types (flat and short) occurred with various breath shapes which resulted in a wide range of r values (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from correlation analysis with figure reference

claim: Some USV syllable types are defined by the presence of large, instantaneous jumps in frequency (like the step up, step down, two- and multi-step).
source: Some USV syllable types are defined by the presence of large, instantaneous jumps in frequency (like the step up, step down, two- and multi-step).
evidence: Description of USV characteristics from classification

claim: A jump in frequency was not associated with a corresponding change in airflow.
source: A jump was not associated with a corresponding change in airflow.
evidence: Observation from analysis of airflow and pitch data

claim: The jumps in frequency did not predict the subsequent intonation pattern.
source: Also, the jumps did not predict the subsequent intonation pattern.
evidence: Observation from analysis of pitch patterns

claim: Step up syllables could be negative to negative (20%), negative to positive (20%), or positive to positive (60%) intonations.
source: For example, step up syllables could be negative to negative (20%), negative to positive (20%), or positive to positive (60%) intonations.
evidence: Quantitative categorization of intonation patterns from data analysis

claim: The relationship between airflow and pitch is relative rather than absolute across all USV types.
source: Across all USV types, we found that the relationship between airflow and pitch is relative rather than absolute which is expected since the relationship is determined by at least two independent variables (laryngeal tone and exhalation speed).
evidence: Interpretation of data patterns with mechanistic reasoning

claim: A vocalization pattern generator must integrate with and even control the breath airflow as a key mechanism to produce various USV types in the murine lexicon.
source: This supports the hypothesis that a vocalization pattern generator must integrate with and even control the breath airflow as a key mechanism to produce various USV types in the murine lexicon.
evidence: Hypothesis supported by experimental observations of airflow-pitch correlations

claim: EMG activity during basal breathing displayed the three phases of the breath cycle.
source: EMG activity during basal breathing displayed the three phases of the breath cycle (Yackle, 2023).
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings with citation

claim: The diaphragm was active during inspiration and larynx in the subsequent post-inspiration period, and these were followed by a late expiration phase where neither muscle was active.
source: The diaphragm was active during inspiration and larynx in the subsequent post-inspiration period, and these were followed by a late expiration phase where neither muscle was active (Figure 3A).
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings with figure reference

claim: The airflow measured by plethysmography had an ~10 ms lag when compared to the EMG activities.
source: The airflow measured by plethysmography had an ~10 ms lag when compared to the EMG activities (blue and red arrows, Figure 3A).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from simultaneous recordings

claim: Upon exposure to female odors, the male mice produced bouts of USVs containing the entire lexicon for several minutes.
source: Upon exposure to female odors, the male mice produced bouts of USVs containing the entire lexicon for several minutes, demonstrating that electrodes interfered with neither breathing nor sound production (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observation from EMG experiments with figure reference

claim: Breaths containing USVs were distinguished from adjacent breaths lacking sound by an increase in laryngeal muscle activity that prolonged into expiration.
source: Breaths containing USVs were distinguished from adjacent breaths lacking sound by an increase in laryngeal muscle activity that prolonged into expiration.
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings comparing vocalization and non-vocalization breaths

claim: The sound followed EMG activity by ~10 ms.
source: Like airflow, the sound followed EMG activity by ~10 ms.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from simultaneous recordings

claim: Down fm USVs started later during expiration and began at a drop in expiratory airflow.
source: Down fms started later during expiration and began at a drop in expiratory airflow (Figure 3C).
evidence: Observation from EMG and airflow recordings with figure reference

claim: For down fm USVs, the diaphragm activity occurred just before the decrease in expiratory airflow and the following laryngeal activity persisted during the sound.
source: The diaphragm activity occurred just before the decrease in expiratory airflow (blue arrow, Figure 3C) and the following laryngeal activity persisted during the sound.
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings with figure reference

claim: The pattern of diaphragm then laryngeal activity during down fm USVs reflects the activity of the muscles during a normal breath, inspiration (diaphragm) then post-inspiration (larynx), but this pattern was ectopically embedded within an expiration.
source: This pattern reflects the activity of the muscles during a normal breath, inspiration (diaphragm) then post-inspiration (larynx), but this pattern was ectopically embedded within an expiration.
evidence: Interpretation of EMG patterns comparing vocalization to normal breathing

claim: Complex vocalizations had the diaphragm then laryngeal activity pattern during expiration, but this cycled multiple times concurrent with the increase and decrease in expiratory airflow and pitch.
source: Similarly, complex vocalizations had the diaphragm then laryngeal activity pattern during expiration, but this cycled multiple times concurrent with the increase and decrease in expiratory airflow and pitch (Figure 3C).
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings with figure reference

claim: Complex USVs had an average of 1.5 cycles per expiration.
source: Complex USVs had an average of 1.5 cycles per expiration
evidence: Quantitative measurement from EMG data analysis

claim: The interval between diaphragm bursts during complex USVs was 43±14 ms.
source: the interval between diaphragm bursts was 43±14 ms
evidence: Quantitative measurement from EMG data analysis

claim: The laryngeal activity during complex USVs occurred at 69 ± 12% through the diaphragm-to-diaphragm interval.
source: and the laryngeal activity occurred at 69 ± 12% through this diaphragm-to-diaphragm interval.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from EMG data analysis

claim: In ~19% of the complex USVs, sound, laryngeal, and diaphragm activity co-occurred.
source: Also, in ~19% of the complex USVs, sound, laryngeal, and diaphragm activity co-occurred, suggesting that other mechanisms contribute to the diversity of sounds.
evidence: Quantitative observation from EMG data with interpretation

claim: For up fm USVs, at the peak of the post-inspiratory period of the breath, the vocalization began and persisted throughout the laryngeal muscle activity.
source: At the peak of the post-inspiratory period of the breath, the vocalization began and persisted throughout the laryngeal muscle activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings with figure reference

claim: For up fm USVs, the sound ended at the onset of a burst in the diaphragm EMG.
source: The sound ended at the onset of a burst in the diaphragm EMG (Figure 3C).
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings with figure reference

claim: Ectopic activation of antiphase patterns of inspiratory and post-inspiratory muscles during the expiration of a vocal breath appears to result in a USV with positive intonation.
source: Ectopic activation of these antiphase patterns during the expiration of a vocal breath appears to result in a USV with positive intonation and the cyclic engagement of this leads to an oscillating pitch.
evidence: Interpretation of EMG patterns and their relationship to pitch

claim: The cyclic engagement of antiphase patterns of inspiratory and post-inspiratory muscles leads to an oscillating pitch.
source: Ectopic activation of these antiphase patterns during the expiration of a vocal breath appears to result in a USV with positive intonation and the cyclic engagement of this leads to an oscillating pitch.
evidence: Interpretation of EMG patterns and their relationship to pitch

claim: The termination of the USV with negative intonation corresponds to the re-activation of inspiratory muscles.
source: Additionally, the termination of the USV with negative intonation corresponds to the re-activation of inspiratory muscles (Figure 3D).
evidence: Observation from EMG recordings with figure reference

claim: The endogenous pattern of the breathing CPG is re-engaged within an adult vocal breath, a 'mini-breath', which mimics the rhythmic syllables of the neonatal vocalizations patterned by the iRO.
source: The novel finding that the endogenous pattern of the breathing CPG is re-engaged within an adult vocal breath, a 'mini-breath', mimics the rhythmic syllables of the neonatal vocalizations patterned by the iRO (Wei et al., 2022).
evidence: Interpretation of EMG patterns with comparison to cited prior work

claim: The iRO also plays a central role in the production of adult vocalizations.
source: This suggests that the iRO also plays a central role in the production of adult vocalizations.
evidence: Inference from similarity of adult and neonatal vocalization patterns

claim: The iRO is molecularly defined in the neonate by the co-expression of Preproenkephalin (Penk) and Vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (Slc17a6).
source: The iRO is molecularly defined in the neonate by the co-expression of Preproenkephalin (Penk) and Vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (Slc17a6) and is anatomically localized to the medullary ventral intermediate reticular formation (iRT) directly medial to the compact nucleus ambiguus (NA) (Wei et al., 2022).
evidence: Definition from cited prior work

claim: The iRO is anatomically localized to the medullary ventral intermediate reticular formation (iRT) directly medial to the compact nucleus ambiguus (NA).
source: The iRO is molecularly defined in the neonate by the co-expression of Preproenkephalin (Penk) and Vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (Slc17a6) and is anatomically localized to the medullary ventral intermediate reticular formation (iRT) directly medial to the compact nucleus ambiguus (NA) (Wei et al., 2022).
evidence: Definition from cited prior work

claim: tdTomato+ and YFP+ Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons were found in the iRT adjacent to the compact NA in adult mice.
source: Consistent with the definition of the iRO in neonatal mice, tdTomato+ and YFP+ Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons were found in the iRT adjacent to the compact NA (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Observation from anatomical experiments with figure reference

claim: The ventrolateral medulla of adult mice contains neurons with the molecular and anatomical identity of the iRO.
source: These results demonstrate that the ventrolateral medulla of adult mice contains neurons with the molecular and anatomical identity of the iRO.
evidence: Conclusion from anatomical and molecular labeling experiments

claim: Neonatal iRO neurons are presynaptic to the kernel of breathing, the pacemaker for inspiration (preBötzinger complex [preBötC]).
source: Neonatal iRO neurons are presynaptic to the kernel of breathing, the pacemaker for inspiration (preBötzinger complex [preBötC]) (Smith et al., 1991), and premotor to multiple laryngeal and tongue muscles.
evidence: Statement about neonatal iRO connectivity with citation

claim: Neonatal iRO neurons are premotor to multiple laryngeal and tongue muscles.
source: Neonatal iRO neurons are presynaptic to the kernel of breathing, the pacemaker for inspiration (preBötzinger complex [preBötC]) (Smith et al., 1991), and premotor to multiple laryngeal and tongue muscles.
evidence: Statement about neonatal iRO connectivity

claim: YFP+ axons of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons elaborated within the NA and RAm where laryngeal premotor and motor neurons localize.
source: We traced the YFP+ axons of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons (Penk-Cre; Slc17a6-Flp and AAV CreONFlpON-ChR2::YFP) and found they elaborated within the NA and RAm where laryngeal premotor and motor neurons localize (Figure 4A and D)
evidence: Observation from anatomical tracing experiments with figure reference

claim: YFP+ axons of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons elaborated within the breathing pacemaker.
source: We traced the YFP+ axons of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons (Penk-Cre; Slc17a6-Flp and AAV CreONFlpON-ChR2::YFP) and found they elaborated within the NA and RAm where laryngeal premotor and motor neurons localize (Figure 4A and D), the breathing pacemaker (Figure 4E)
evidence: Observation from anatomical tracing experiments with figure reference

claim: YFP+ axons of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons elaborated within the hypoglossal (tongue) motor nucleus.
source: We traced the YFP+ axons of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons (Penk-Cre; Slc17a6-Flp and AAV CreONFlpON-ChR2::YFP) and found they elaborated within the NA and RAm where laryngeal premotor and motor neurons localize (Figure 4A and D), the breathing pacemaker (Figure 4E), and the hypoglossal (tongue) motor nucleus (Figure 4E).
evidence: Observation from anatomical tracing experiments with figure reference

claim: The projection patterns of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons provide additional evidence that these adult neurons maintain the same connectivity properties as the neonatal iRO neurons.
source: The projection patterns of these Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons provide additional evidence that these adult neurons maintain the same connectivity properties as the neonatal iRO neurons, indicating they can control the key elements for vocalization: the breath airflow and larynx.
evidence: Interpretation of anatomical tracing results

claim: Adult Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons can control the key elements for vocalization: the breath airflow and larynx.
source: The projection patterns of these Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons provide additional evidence that these adult neurons maintain the same connectivity properties as the neonatal iRO neurons, indicating they can control the key elements for vocalization: the breath airflow and larynx.
evidence: Inference from anatomical connectivity to functional capability

claim: In adult mice, vocalizations have been triggered by activation of the midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG), namely glutamatergic neurons in the lateral to ventrolateral subregion.
source: In adult mice, vocalizations have been triggered by activation of the midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG), namely glutamatergic neurons in the lateral to ventrolateral subregion (Michael et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021; Tschida et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citations

claim: YFP+ neurons from the ipsi- and contralateral PAG projected to the iRO region in nearly equal numbers.
source: Among the labeled brain regions, we found YFP+ neurons in a region of the midbrain PAG overlapping with areas that contain PAG-USV neurons. To our surprise, neurons from the ipsi- and contralateral PAG projected to the iRO region in nearly equal numbers (Figure 4F).
evidence: Observation from retrograde tracing experiments with figure reference

claim: The iRO exists in adults and is embedded within the brainstem phonation network (PAG → iRO → the preBötC, NA, RAm, hypoglossal).
source: These molecular, anatomical, and neural morphology characterizations reveal that the iRO exists in adults and is embedded within the brainstem phonation network (PAG → iRO → the preBötC, NA, RAm, hypoglossal) (Figure 4G).
evidence: Conclusion from multiple anatomical and molecular experiments

claim: Ectopic light activation of the Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons induced bouts of vocalizations where the breathing rate was entrained by the frequency of stimulation.
source: In both instances we implanted optic fibers above the iRO bilaterally to further localize neural activation (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). In both experimental regimes, ectopic light activation of the Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons induced bouts of vocalizations where the breathing rate was entrained by the frequency of stimulation (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Observation from optogenetic experiments with figure references

claim: Most bouts and the breaths within contained vocalizations during optogenetic stimulation of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons.
source: Most bouts and the breaths within contained vocalizations (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Quantitative observation from optogenetic experiments with figure references

claim: The amplitudes of all elicited breaths were significantly increased during optogenetic stimulation of Penk+Slc17a6+ neurons.
source: and the amplitudes of all elicited breaths were significantly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Quantitative observation from optogenetic experiments with figure reference

claim: Some AAV-ChR2 mice showed previously described broad-band harmonic vocalizations, while others did not vocalize (n=5/9), likely due to incomplete labeling.
source: Some AAV-ChR2 mice showed previously described broad-band harmonic vocalizations (like Grimsley et al., 2011), while others did not vocalize (n=5/9), likely due to incomplete labeling.
evidence: Observation from optogenetic experiments with interpretation

claim: The ReaChR animals without vocalizations were found to have 'off-target' optic fiber implants (n=2/6).
source: Additionally, the ReaChR animals without vocalizations were found to have 'off-target' optic fiber implants (n=2/6).
evidence: Observation from post-hoc anatomical verification

claim: The iRO is sufficient to induce phonation via control of both breath airflow and laryngeal opening.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with the notion that the iRO is sufficient to induce phonation via control of both breath airflow and laryngeal opening, just as it does in neonatal cries.
evidence: Conclusion from optogenetic experiments with comparison to neonatal function

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of glutamatergic preBötC neurons never elicited vocalizations, although breathing sped up.
source: First, to ensure that just stimulation of breathing is insufficient to elicit vocalization, we optogenetically excited the glutamatergic preBötC neurons (Slc17a6-Cre with AAV CreON-ChR2). Indeed, we found that, although breathing sped up, optogenetic stimulation never elicited vocalizations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, H, I).
evidence: Observation from control optogenetic experiments with figure references

claim: Activation of Penk+, µ-opioid receptor+Slc17a6+, Tachykinin 1+, and Vesicular GABA transporter+ neurons never induced vocalizations, although breathing was altered in various ways.
source: And second, to determine if the ability to elicit vocalizations was generalizable to other neural types in the iRO anatomical region, we activated Penk+, µ-opioid receptor+Slc17a6+, Tachykinin 1+, and Vesicular GABA transporter+neurons and found that vocalizations were never induced upon light stimulation, although breathing was altered in various ways (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from control optogenetic experiments with figure reference

claim: Seven of the ten types of endogenous USVs were induced upon activation of the iRO.
source: We classified the evoked iRO vocalizations (Penk-Cre;Slc17a6-Flp;CreONFlpON-ReaChR) with the CNN, and to our surprise, seven of the ten types of endogenous USVs were induced upon activation of the iRO (Figure 5).
evidence: Observation from optogenetic experiments with CNN classification

claim: The most abundant elicited USV was the down fm which, in the endogenous dataset, had the strongest positive intonation.
source: The most abundant elicited USV was the down fm which, in the endogenous dataset, had the strongest positive intonation (Figure 5G and Figure 2).
evidence: Observation from optogenetic experiments compared to endogenous data

claim: The down fm is the least common endogenous USV and up fm is the most common.
source: These results are striking since the down fm is the least common endogenous USV and up fm is the most common (Figure 1).
evidence: Observation from endogenous vocalization data with figure reference

claim: The optically evoked USV types were biased toward those with endogenous positive intonation.
source: These results are consistent with the first prediction where the optically evoked USV types were biased toward those with endogenous positive intonation.
evidence: Interpretation comparing optogenetic results to predictions

claim: All the ectopic USVs combined had a more positive association between airflow and pitch compared to all endogenous USVs.
source: Beyond this, all the ectopic USVs combined had a more positive association between airflow and pitch compared to all endogenous USVs (Figure 5D).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of correlation coefficients with figure reference

claim: The positive bias in optogenetically evoked USVs was not explained purely by the abundance of down fm since when these were omitted from the analysis the positive bias was unchanged.
source: This was not explained purely by the abundance of down fm since when these were omitted from the analysis the positive bias was unchanged.
evidence: Result from statistical analysis controlling for USV type

claim: The iRO is sufficient to pattern nearly all USV types.
source: These data demonstrate that the iRO is sufficient to pattern nearly all USV types, and that the pitch of the induced vocalizations tightly follows the breathing airflow.
evidence: Conclusion from optogenetic experiments

claim: The pitch of the induced vocalizations tightly follows the breathing airflow.
source: These data demonstrate that the iRO is sufficient to pattern nearly all USV types, and that the pitch of the induced vocalizations tightly follows the breathing airflow.
evidence: Conclusion from correlation analysis of optogenetically evoked USVs

claim: The intonation that establishes the diversity of the adult murine lexicon is explained by two mechanisms, the modulation of the breath waveform and presumably the size of the laryngeal opening.
source: Here, we propose that the intonation that establishes the diversity of the adult murine lexicon is explained by two mechanisms, the modulation of the breath waveform and presumably the size of the laryngeal opening.
evidence: Summary statement of main proposal based on experimental findings

claim: Unique vocalization types have characteristic fluctuations in the expiratory airflow, whereby some changes in pitch are strongly correlated with airflow (positive intonation) while others are anti-correlated (negative intonation).
source: We describe that unique vocalization types have characteristic fluctuations in the expiratory airflow, whereby some changes in pitch are strongly correlated with airflow (positive intonation) while others are anti-correlated (negative intonation).
evidence: Summary of correlation analysis results

claim: The two mechanisms of positive and negative intonation can be used in the same breath to produce complex changes in pitch.
source: These two mechanisms can even be used in the same breath to produce complex changes in pitch.
evidence: Observation from analysis of two step and step up USVs

claim: Seven of the ten USV types primarily used the positive intonation mechanism.
source: To our surprise, seven of the ten USV types primarily used the positive intonation mechanism.
evidence: Summary of correlation analysis results

claim: Re-activation of the breathing CPG during the expiration phase of the vocal breath appeared as a 'mini-breath' (inspiratory diaphragm then post-inspiratory laryngeal muscle activities) nested within a normal expiration and corresponded with modulated airflow and pitch.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found re-activation of the breathing CPG during the expiration phase of the vocal breath. This ectopic activity appeared as a 'mini-breath' (inspiratory diaphragm then post-inspiratory laryngeal muscle activities) nested within a normal expiration and corresponded with modulated airflow and pitch.
evidence: Summary of EMG findings

claim: The iRO is sufficient to induce most of the endogenous USV syllable types via the modulation of the breath airflow.
source: We show that the iRO is sufficient to induce most of the endogenous USV syllable types via the modulation of the breath airflow.
evidence: Summary of optogenetic experimental results

claim: In contrast to the natural lexicon, the pitch of the evoked USVs is primarily explained by positive intonation.
source: In contrast to the natural lexicon, the pitch of the evoked USVs is primarily explained by positive intonation.
evidence: Summary of correlation analysis comparing optogenetic and endogenous USVs

claim: The iRO can produce the mechanism to pattern positive intonation.
source: These data imply that the iRO can produce the mechanism to pattern positive intonation, thereby suggesting that negative intonation derives from a separate neuronal component of the phonatory system.
evidence: Inference from optogenetic results showing bias toward positive intonation

claim: Negative intonation derives from a separate neuronal component of the phonatory system.
source: These data imply that the iRO can produce the mechanism to pattern positive intonation, thereby suggesting that negative intonation derives from a separate neuronal component of the phonatory system.
